title: Nordic Perspectives on Education: A Two-Book Launch
content:
The books  (Brill) and (Stockholm University Press) present current knowledge on the research and practice of moral and citizenship education and of gifted education in the Nordic countries: Denmark, Iceland, Finland, Norway and Sweden. The Nordic countries share a common social and cultural history, together with a commitment to human rights and to the principles of non-discrimination, social justice, respect for life, human dignity and cultural diversity.

How are these values realised in the Nordic model of education and in the policy of “one school for all”? What kind of research and practice is needed in these fields today? And how can Nordic co-operation advance research and teaching across the Nordic countries?

Professor Kirsi Tirri (University of Helsinki) presents Nordic Perspectives on Moral and Citizenship Education, and Professor Valerie Margrain (Karlstad University) presents Nordic Perspectives on Gifted Education. A panel discussion follows the presentations, and the event closes with questions from the audience.

title: Anna Maria Fjordbøge discussed ethnographic findings on digitalisation and judicial independence
content:
In her presentation, “Blurring boundaries? Negotiating digitalization, efficiency efforts and tripartition of power at the Danish courts” Fjordbøge discussed the ongoing digitalisation of the Danish courts and the penal chain.

The presentation drew on findings from a year-long ethnographic fieldwork project examining how digitalisation and efforts to improve the efficiency of court processes are discussed and implemented in the Danish judiciary. Particular attention was paid to debates concerning the constitutionality of recent digitalisation initiatives, as well as to interactions between administrative and managerial professionals and legal professionals.

A central theme of the presentation was judicial independence. Fjordbøge approached independence as an essentially contested concept within the Danish judiciary and legal policy: different groups of actors may attach different meanings to what judicial independence entails and how it should be protected in practice.

title: Jeffrey Barrettin tavoitteena on sairauksien havaitseminen aiemmin ja tarkemmin
content:
Jeffrey Barrett, the new Professor of Computational Predictive Medicine at the University of Helsinki and ELLIS Institute Finland, has a career spanning genomics, public health and industry. He uses AI methods and large-scale health data to identify practical and clinically relevant biomarkers.

For Barrett, the professorship represents a return to academia after several years in industry, but also an opportunity to bring new ways of thinking into academic research.

"I've been fortunate to have worked both in academia and in companies, and I think there is a lot we can learn from both worlds," he says.

Computational predictive medicine combines large-scale health data, molecular measurements and advanced AI methods to uncover biological signatures of disease. Rather than simply predicting who may become ill, the goal is to recognise emerging disease processes earlier and identify the patients most likely to benefit from preventive treatments.

title: Symposium: Indigenous Relationships with Time
content:
The MultiBEING Justice Centre of Excellence will kick-off at the University of Helsinki. CoE organizes its first scientific symposium on Monday September 28th, 2026 and engages with Indigenous notions of time by distinguished international speakers. 

The symposium addresses the connections and lineages of beings. Conceptions of time shape how relationships with other beings are lived, valued, and perceived. Non-linear time is a key aspect of understanding Indigenous relational onto-epistemologies. The speakers foreground philosophies of time, seasonalities, traditional calendars, ancestralities, astronomy, and diverse temporalities and timelines. What role do they play in reconsidering multibeing flourishing and human responsibility beyond humans?

title: Southnord Artfest 2026: Roots En Route
content:
Roots En Route is a multi-sensory installation by four artists who will create a multi-sensory installation in dialogue with the greenhouses – examining rootedness and displacement; asking what grows where it was planted and what survives the crossing. The African plants that fill the greenhouses carry their own histories of movement and adaptation.

Camille Norment in collaboration with Sofia Jernberg create a soundscape drawing on the insects and birds of the plants' homelands. Toubab Holmes' site-specific scent installation traces the hidden journeys of plants through the extractive system of perfumery. Charmaine Watkiss visits the botanical legacies and healing traditions of her Caribbean ancestry through large-scale drawings of Plant Warriors. Together, the three works read the botanical garden as an archive of movement, and the plants in it as things that were carried, taken and made to travel.

Running from October 2026 through January 2027, the exhibition offers a long, unhurried encounter between art and the plant world. Set aside more time than you think you need. Walk slowly, sense carefully, and let yourself be immersed.

title: Uusi maisteriohjelma tarjoaa ruokaviennin kansainvälistä osaamista
content:
The English-language Master’s Programme in International Food Business and Gastronomy equips students with relevant skills in branding, export, gastronomy and sustainability. 

This two-year programme centres on international food business including management and marketing, and covers sustainable food systems, logistics and food legislation. In addition, students learn to understand gastronomic markets, develop new gastronomy products and services and introduce them to new markets. 

Graduates from the programme can pursue careers in international food companies, working, for instance, as brand and product, export or marketing managers. Other options include key account management roles in retail, or setting up one’s own food-sector startup.

While the expertise developed also applies well to NGOs, public-sector organisations and research institutes involved in food systems, the programme equally prepares students for postgraduate study and academic careers.

title: “Ilman pölyttäjiä maailma olisi ankea ja väritön” – Uusi näyttely avaa oven pölyttäjien kiehtovaan elämään
content:
Pollinators represent an astonishingly diverse group of animals, many of which possess remarkable abilities despite their small size. Bees can count, bumblebees solve problems, and on distant islands, even lizards can pollinate flowers.

The  exhibition, which combines science and art, offers a wealth of information, stunning visuals, and fun activities for visitors of all ages. Guests can play interactive games like "Identify the Pollinators" and "Pollinator Protection Bingo," design their own imaginary pollinator, and explore the museum's impressive collection of specimens. The exhibition is based on a newly illustrated non-fiction book.

– We want to show the world through the eyes of pollinators, says exhibition scriptwriter Mia Rönkä, Adjunct Professor in Environmental Ecology at the University of Turku. Rönkä has written the exhibition’s informational texts and poems.

Although the sensory perceptions, cognitive abilities, and communication methods of pollinators like bees differ from ours as humans, we can still strive to understand and appreciate them as individuals of other species – without anthropomorphizing them, Rönkä explains.

title: Arkadiankadun siltaremontti aiheuttaa muutoksia liikennejärjestelyihin Luonnontieteellisen museon lähistöllä
content:
The renovation will start with the construction of temporary traffic arrangements from Wednesday 7 January onwards. The renovation is expected to be completed in late 2026.

A temporary bridge for pedestrians will be built on the east side of Arkadiankatu over the Baana. The aim is to maintain the pedestrian route on the east side of the bridge until the temporary bridge is operational. Cyclists will also be able to use the bridge.

The Baana route underneath the bridge is expected to remain open for most of the renovation's duration, with some minor exceptions.

There will be changes to the motor vehicle routes by the bridge and around it in January. If possible, should be favoured during the bridge renovation.

Connections to the bus terminals in Kamppi will remain available, but there will be a slight diversion of routes.

Trams 1 and 1T will run via Simonkatu and Kamppi. Lasipalatsi and the Natural History Museum will not be served.

The diversion is due to the renovation of the Arkadiankatu bridge and will remain in place until late 2026. The renovation will not affect HSL's bus services.

title: Ukrainan sota - yliopiston suositukset
content:
The University of Helsinki has condemned the military action by Russia and expressed its support for Ukraine and its university community. We have also expressed our support for Ukraine, together with other Finnish universities, through statements by and the . As a demonstration of support, we have illuminated buildings in the colours of the Ukrainian flag and raised the flag on our premises.

One of the principles of the University of Helsinki is to promote international collaboration in research and higher education, and to support these efforts even in difficult circumstances. Russia’s indefensible military aggression in Ukraine has required exceptional measures, which include those taken in the collaboration between universities.

The University of Helsinki is monitoring both national and EU-level sanctions, adapting our policies and processes accordingly. Together with other Finnish and international universities, the University of Helsinki strives to promote the end of military action in Ukraine, while supporting Ukrainian institutions and people.

title: Olkapään rakenteellisia muutoksia löytyy lähes kaikilta yli 40-vuotiailta
content:
How common are abnormal shoulder imaging findings among the general population and do they explain shoulder pain? The question is fundamental, since even though shoulders have been scanned for decades, there has been no reliable information on what is normal.

Researchers took X-ray and MRI scans of both shoulders of 602 Finns. Aged between 41 and 76 years of age, the participants were randomly selected from the nationally representative Health 2000 dataset. In other words, none of the participants sought treatment because of symptoms.

The result was unambiguous: 99% of Finns over 40 had at least one abnormal finding in the rotator cuff, a structure composed of four tendons that move and support the shoulder. The findings ranged from mild degenerative changes to the most severe degree, full-thickness tears, the latter identified in 11% of participants. Osteoarthritis of the shoulder was found in 39% of cases. Findings became more numerous and severe with age.

“We expected the findings to be common but not that they would be practically universal. We were not expecting 99 percent,” says Doctoral Researcher Thomas Ibounig from the University of Helsinki’s Faculty of Medicine.
